name: Aldous Harding
label: 4AD
lede: A busker from Geraldine who sings in about six different voices, keeps her lyrics to herself, and has now made three of her five albums at the same Welsh studio with the same producer.

eras.title: A fearful kid, a folk farm, a busker's break
eras.text: Hannah Topp grows up between Dunedin and a flaxseed farm in Geraldine, sings on her mother's record at 13, and busks her way into the Lyttelton scene near Christchurch. The debut is being made in a makeshift studio while the city is still shaking.

years.h: Hannah Sian Topp is born, and later borrows a stepfather's name
years.p: Her mother is the Canadian-born folk singer [[Lorina Harding|1053f346-3f4b-4277-a18a-9ffab48b66ef]]. 'Aldous' came from wanting something that sounded like a manly Alice, according to Wikipedia.
years.xp:
Wikipedia gives her birthplace as Lyttelton; AudioCulture and a 2014 interview have her born in Auckland and raised in Dunedin until she was 11, then on an organic flaxseed farm outside Geraldine. The farm hosted an annual folk festival, and she headlined the last one in 2016.

Harding is her stepfather's surname. She has described herself as a fearful, lonely kid who danced in her pyjamas to the radio.

years.h: At 13 she sings on her mother's album Clean Break
years.p: The record won a Tui for best folk album. Wikipedia lists the song as 'Exactly What to Say'.
years.xp: AudioCulture says she resisted a music career for years because she tied it to being poor, separated, and not being home. She finished school at Logan Park High School in Dunedin, singing with her friends [[Nadia Reid|2485f75b-bbac-4c9d-8bf2-da323bd7ccfa]] and Flora Knight, and wrote her first songs as poems she couldn't accompany.

years.h: Busking in Christchurch, she gets pulled onstage the same night
years.p: Adam McGrath of [[The Eastern|69b718c9-4979-4bd7-9ca0-e9b3a8e6644c]] heard her in the street and had her sing with the band at the Wunderbar in Lyttelton that evening.
years.xp: McGrath remembered that she 'made everyone lose their breath with her voice and attitude and of course her bravery.' After travelling in Europe and Quebec she rejoined the band a year later and played with them for a couple of years, opening for Old Crow Medicine Show and Fleetwood Mac, according to NZ Musician.

years.big: Where creative types go to die
q: Where creative types go to die
years.h: Lyttelton takes her in, and she says what it costs
years.p: Harding on the port town's other side: 'a lot of drugs and alcohol.' She moved there at the end of 2008 and still calls it the place she feels most at home.
years.xp: Wikipedia quotes her on the harbour town near Christchurch: it is 'sort of where sometimes it feels like that's where creative types go to die.' She also says the region is where she feels most at home anywhere. Through The Eastern she met the producer Ben Edwards and the singer [[Marlon Williams|92677e54-c738-4e33-8c08-e51ba490285b]].

years.h: Busking in Cashel Mall when the Christchurch earthquake hits
years.p: She was unhurt and went home to Geraldine. That October a bakery busk got her an opening slot for Anika Moa, who lent her a week of recording space in Auckland.
years.xp: Those Auckland recordings were never released, according to AudioCulture. The debut she started with Edwards and Williams was interrupted by the February 2011 quake and picked up again the following year.

years.cap: Aldous Harding at the Old Queen's Head, Nov 2016 · Wikimedia
years.h: A concrete room under a supermarket, and a debut in pieces
years.p: Harding records with Ben Edwards and [[Marlon Williams|92677e54-c738-4e33-8c08-e51ba490285b]] in a makeshift Lyttelton studio; part of it was cut under the Wunderbar, which had no toilet.
years.xp:
AudioCulture puts the sessions in a concrete studio beneath the Lyttelton supermarket; in a 2014 interview she says part of the record was made under the Wunderbar and part at Edwards's studio. Edwards was an old friend.

She described the finished record as a story of a battle between good and evil that's in everybody. The oldest song, 'Hunter', was about four years old by then.

eras.title: Out of Lyttelton, into Bristol
eras.text: The debut comes out on Lyttelton Records with Flying Nun behind it, and Harding follows Williams to Melbourne, where a friend puts her in touch with the producer who will shape everything after.

years.h: Aldous Harding · Lyttelton Records / Flying Nun
years.p: Nine songs of gothic folk, released through Lyttelton Records and the Flying Nun label. It reached number 35 in New Zealand, per Wikipedia.
years.xp:
Critic Nick Bollinger, quoted by AudioCulture, said her voice 'shifted the air with rarefied grace.' Around this time her live sets included a cover of Toto's 'Africa', she told Witchdoctor.

Later, she said she had no idea how that sound came out of her on the early songs.

years.h: Melbourne, and a tip from Laura Jean
years.p: Harding moves to Melbourne after Williams. The musician [[Laura Jean|4bb7a54a-00a6-46eb-b054-df54895695ee]] puts her in touch with [[John Parish|4ae92e70-3690-473b-8fbc-49749565669f]], the man behind [[PJ Harvey|e795e03d-b5d5-4a5f-834d-162cfb308a2c]]'s records.
years.xp: AudioCulture reports that Laura Jean made the connection. Parish, born in 1959, co-founded Automatic Dlamini in 1982; PJ Harvey played in it from 1988 to 1991, and the two made Dance Hall at Louse Point in 1996.

years.cap: Aldous Harding at Paper Dress Vintage · Wikimedia
q: We rub up against each other like two old porcupines.
years.h: Bristol: two porcupines and a studio called J & J
years.p: Harding flies to England to record Party with Parish at J & J Studio, with [[Fenne Lily|cd295735-b68a-4b5d-aa10-de0dea37ca89]] and [[Perfume Genius|c4ff10e0-ae5a-467d-a409-6e0b4bf241eb]]'s Mike Hadreas guesting.
years.xp: Harding called Parish gentle and patient, but said that they 'rub up against each other like two old porcupines.' That working relationship would run to Party, Designer, Warm Chris and Train on the Island.

eras.title: Party, and the 4AD deal
eras.text: 4AD announces the signing and puts out Party worldwide alongside Flying Nun. The videos get stranger, the voice keeps changing character, and the awards start.

years.src: Wikipedia: Party (Aldous Harding album) · Wikipedia: Aldous Harding · AudioCulture
years.h: Party · 4AD / Flying Nun
years.p: The first 4AD album, produced by Parish. 'Horizon' came out as the first single on 10 February.
years.xp:
Party charted at number 6 in New Zealand and won the 2017 NZ Music Awards for Breakthrough Artist and Alternative. Metacritic gives it 83 from 11 reviews; The Guardian called her 'one of the most original songwriters around', and Jon Pareles of The New York Times said her exposed voice 'changes character from song to song'.

She played 'Horizon' on BBC Two's Later... with Jools Holland the same evening as [[Lorde|8e494408-8620-4c6a-82c2-c2ca4a1e4f12]], and AudioCulture says the studio lights magnified her facial quirks.

years.h: 'Imagining My Man' brings in Mike Hadreas
years.p: Perfume Genius's Hadreas sings on the second single from Party, in a video directed by Charlotte Evans.

years.src: Wikipedia: Aldous Harding · AudioCulture · Wikipedia: Party (Aldous Harding album)
years.h: Party wins the Taite Prize
years.p: New Zealand's album of the year prize for a record made in Bristol by a Lyttelton busker.
years.xp: AudioCulture adds that 'Horizon' was runner-up for the APRA Silver Scroll, narrowly losing to Lorde. The 'Blend' video, in a cowgirl look AudioCulture compares to Apocalypse Now, arrived on 12 June 2017.

eras.title: Designer and the Silver Scroll
eras.text: She swaps the sad-girl frame for shuffling beats and a Welsh backing band, and writes a song that wins New Zealand's top songwriting prize.

years.h: Designer · 4AD / Flying Nun
years.p: Recorded at Rockfield Studios in Wales with Parish, and with [[H. Hawkline|ae41819a-51e2-4f21-aa3c-b37f22b733ae]] on bass, guitar and keyboards.
years.xp:
AudioCulture says she recruited musicians from [[Cate Le Bon|f2393e49-b791-46da-a6d7-1e9e60743405]]'s band, Hawkline (Huw Evans) among them, and a levity and playfulness that hadn't been there before. Pitchfork gave it 8.0 and Metacritic averages 88; it reached number 5 in New Zealand.

Wikipedia lists the extras: saxophone from Stephen Black and violin from Clare Mactaggart.

years.cap: Aldous Harding at Haldern Pop Festival 2017 · Wikimedia
years.h: 'The Barrel' wins the 2019 APRA Silver Scroll
years.p: New Zealand's songwriting award goes to a song whose meaning she declines to explain.
years.xp: Designer was a finalist for the 2020 Taite Music Prize and won the Alternative category at the 2019 NZ Music Awards. Harding has said she tries not to explain her songs: 'I know exactly what my songs are about, and I try not to tell people.'

eras.title: Cardiff, an actor's answer, and a number one
eras.text: She writes at her mother's house in lockdown, lands in Cardiff near H. Hawkline, and cuts Warm Chris at Rockfield. It's her first number one at home.

years.h: Lockdown in Geraldine, then Cardiff
years.p: She writes Warm Chris songs at her mother's place, then settles in the Welsh capital where Hawkline lives.
years.xp: RNZ says much of the record was written during 2020's lockdown at her mother's home in Geraldine before she went to Wales to record. AudioCulture has her settling in Cardiff that year.

years.h: Warm Chris · 4AD / Flying Nun
years.p: Her first New Zealand number one, made at Rockfield Studios in Monmouthshire with Parish and Hawkline.
years.xp: Pitchfork's Sophie Kemp praised 'some of Harding's best songwriting yet', and AudioCulture reports the score as 8.2. Metacritic averages 82; Clash gave 9/10. 'Tick Tock' reached number 31 on the New Zealand singles chart and 'Ennui' 40.

q: I really do feel more like an actor.
years.h: Asked what she is, she says actor
years.p: In an RNZ interview around Warm Chris, Harding says she resonates less and less with the word musician.
years.xp: 'A musician is something that I resonate with less and less,' she told RNZ. She also said listeners don't need to know what she was thinking and that explaining could be detrimental. Her clips, including the ones with director Martin Sagadin, lean on the acting.

years.h: Jason Williamson of Sleaford Mods guests on 'Leathery Whip'
years.p: The Nottingham ranter [[Jason Williamson|efb4c486-56b3-4b1f-a7e8-0cd4e65a9ee7]] appears on the closing track of Warm Chris.
years.xp: RNZ has Harding saying she was drawn to the [[Sleaford Mods|09d8290b-6ada-422f-8ce3-19349fb1c15d]] frontman's physicality and power. Wikipedia credits Williamson as a guest vocalist.

years.h: Tramshed, Cardiff: Hawkline opens, then plays in her band
years.p: Huw Evans warms up alone with an electric guitar and a tape machine; Harding's set includes 'Fever' and 'The Barrel'.
years.xp: Buzz's review of the night says Hawkline's 26-minute solo set drew on his 2023 album Milk for Flowers and 'rawness in his voice'. Harding's band, with him in it, followed her 'shapeshifting voice'.

eras.title: Train on the Island
eras.text: Four years after Warm Chris, Harding returns with her fifth record, again with Parish at Rockfield, and Pitchfork calls it her best.

years.src: Rolling Stone Australia · Brighton and Hove News
years.h: 'One Stop' leads the fifth album
years.p: The video is directed by Michelle Henning. The song premiered on BBC 6 Music's Huw Stephens show.
years.xp: The announcement came with her first headline shows since 2023, and with a limited run of just 50 copies on 'Holiday Records Copper' vinyl, per Rolling Stone Australia.

years.src: Stereogum: Aldous Harding & H. Hawkline · Paste · God Is In The TV
years.h: 'Venus in the Zinnia' is a duet with H. Hawkline
years.p: The video mixes FaceTime footage of the two with Harding floating over the earth.
years.xp: Stereogum credits the video to Harding, Martin Sagadin, Hopey Parish and Michelle Henning, and notes John Parish's Wurlitzer. God Is In The TV and Stereogum both call it a duet with Hawkline; Paste has Parish as the partner.

years.src: Wikipedia: Train on the Island · Paste · Stereogum: Aldous Harding Announces
years.h: Train on the Island · 4AD / Flying Nun
years.p: Pitchfork gives it 9.0 and Best New Music; Jayson Greene calls it her career-best album.
years.xp:
Ten songs in 39 minutes, cut at Rockfield with Parish, Hawkline, drummer Seb Rochford of Polar Bear, harpist Mali Llywelyn, synth player Thomas Poli and pedal steel player Joe Harvey-Whyte. Metacritic averages 87 from 14 reviews, and it reached number 4 in New Zealand.

Paste's Miranda Wollen calls it a 'silly, colorful triumph'. Under the Radar's Mark Moody calls it a mixed bag. 'Coats', the closer, came out as a single two days before the album.

years.src: Brighton and Hove News · Rolling Stone Australia
years.h: Two Barbican nights sell out fast; a third gets added
years.p: UK and European dates run May to August with Vera Ellen supporting. North America follows in September and October.
years.xp: Brighton and Hove News lists the Dome on 25 May and the added London show on 31 May.
